editorNote: Software is leaving the hobby shelf for a billion-dollar contest of packaging, advertising, retail space and price.
morningLine: The machine may sit on the desk, but the software business now wants the whole storefront.

lead.headline: Software's Hard Sell Becomes a Billion-Dollar Business
lead.dek: Commodore readies roughly 70 titles, Lotus buys attention, and software makers learn the arts of packaging and promotion.
lead.confidence: Exact-date reporting for announcements during June 13–19
body: Personal-computer software is becoming a mass-market business before shoppers’ eyes. SRI International estimates that Americans bought $1 billion worth of personal-computer programs in 1982 and forecasts $1.5 billion this year, growth fast enough to turn code once passed among hobbyists into a fiercely promoted consumer product.

Commodore supplied the week’s clearest sign of scale by announcing roughly 70 software titles for summer. Its planned version of Microsoft Multiplan, priced below $100, would undercut versions selling for as much as $275 and put a serious business program within reach of the enormous Commodore home-computer audience.

At the expensive end, Lotus 1-2-3 combines spreadsheet, database and graphing functions for the IBM PC at $495. Time identifies it as the bestselling business program after Lotus backed the launch with a three-month, $1 million advertising campaign—a budget that makes software look increasingly like records, books or packaged goods.

Electronic Arts is making that comparison literal, placing entertainment programs in album-like packages and presenting programmers as “software artists.” Retail is changing too: Software Centre International counts 26 outlets, with 13 more under construction, while experiments in electronic delivery hint that programs may someday reach buyers without a box at all.

stories.headline: Coleco's Adam Resets the Complete-Computer Price
stories.dek: A sub-$600 bundle promises keyboard, storage, printer, software and ColecoVision games.
stories.confidence: Same-month CES announcement; specifications subject to change
body: Coleco’s Adam was the hardware sensation of the Summer Consumer Electronics Show: a complete system promised for under $600, or $450 as an expansion for ColecoVision owners. The announced package joins a Z80A processor, 80K of RAM, detachable keyboard, high-speed 500K digital-data cassette and daisy-wheel printer.

Word processing, Microsoft BASIC, sound, sprites, controllers and Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom round out an unusually complete family package. Contemporary reports caution that final specifications may change before fall and that Applesoft compatibility does not mean most Apple software will run unchanged.

stories.headline: Atari Sweeps the Deck for Four XL Machines
stories.dek: The 600XL and 800XL lead a replacement line built around lower prices and broad compatibility.
body: Atari is replacing the 400, 800 and recently introduced 1200XL with four XL computers while retaining broad compatibility with existing software and peripherals. The 16K 600XL is tagged at $199 and expandable to 64K; the 64K 800XL is listed at $299.

Both bring built-in BASIC, cartridge support, joystick ports, 256 colors and four-channel sound. Atari is also opening its architecture to accessory makers and creating Atari Publishing to sell programs for rival Commodore and Texas Instruments machines.

stories.headline: WarGames Turns Computer Anxiety into a Hit
stories.dek: The computer-centered thriller climbs in its third weekend.
body: WarGames earned $5,355,801 from 973 theaters on June 17–19, an 11 percent rise from the prior weekend. Its domestic total reached $22,260,427 after three weekends.
The thriller ranked fifth nationally behind Superman III, Return of the Jedi, Trading Places and Octopussy, carrying modems, hacking and computer-controlled catastrophe into mainstream conversation.
